Hello, Weihua,
The specific ergm you are fitting is dyad-independent, so it can be fit
using logistic regression. As a result, it never gets to the MCMC
stage, and never produces an MCMC sample.
If you really want an MCMC sample, you can rerun the fit with an
additional control=control.ergm(force.main=TRUE)) argument.
						I hope this helps,	
					Pavel

Thanks in advance,
Rachael

It seems likely to be one of a few factors:

- nearly all ties in the network are homophilous on pasture, so the 
estimate is very high and causing instability

- there is very high correlation between pasture and one of the other 
attributes (breed or use).

diagnose the issue for sure, we can update the list with the final 
insights, for those who are interested.

mixingmatrix(new1, pasture)
mixingmatrix(new1, breed)
mixingmatrix(new1, use)

pasture <- new1%v%'pasture'
breed <- new1%v%'breed'
use <- new1%v%'use'

xtabs(~pasture+breed)
xtabs(~pasture+use)

HTH,

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hello statnet,

In our research, we need to establish the association of three networks
(socialization, perceived competence and perceived value homophily) with
tie-formation in the "focal" network of task advice in an organization (so,
the four networks contain the same node set). We apply ERGMs, to account
for other tie-formation regularities besides the associations of interest.

The problem at hand is missing data: unit non-response, by Huisman's
terminology (2009), i.e. three of 43 actors did not respond to our survey
(they have no outgoing ties recorded), but they were in the survey roster
(so, we do have their incoming ties).

Having in mind that the "covariate networks" have missing data, a "tacit
imputation method" implemented in ergm (statnet) is a no-go for my final
models, since this method assumes no missing information on the fixed
covariates' part.

My question is then how should I approach the missing data imputation, a
priori assuming some ERGM-based imputation is a way to go? More precisely:
am I on the right track with the strategy outlined below, and do you have
some pointers regarding the specific question in the end of the following
section of this message?

I guess I could build four separate ERG models for each of the four
above-mentioned networks (utilizing the tacit imputation method), with all
the usual caveats of model selection and examining GOF. Then I could run
some arbitrary number of simulations constraining the observed edges to
remain unchanged (as described in Section 6, p.15 of PolNet 2011 tutorial
on modeling missing data). I could then use those simulated networks in
further modelling. The problem then is, how to choose which of the
simulated networks should I use out of each set of simulated networks (per
each of the four observed networks)?

What comes to mind is to run ERGMs for all combinations of, let's say, 50
"partly simulated" (imputed) graphs per each of the four networks, and take
mean parameter estimates and standard errors as "true", but this would take
a very long time, and I am not so sure of ERGM statistical underpinnings to
vouchsafe this approach.

What may complicate things even further is that we know (from the truncated
models) that the three covariate networks have some effect on ties of the
focal network, and some of the covariate networks are themselves
"correlated" (we ran separate ERGMs to establish that). It seems to me that
this would in the ideal case call for an imputation procedure that takes
these "associations" into account.

In conclusion, I get the feeling of "trying to use a sledge-hammer to kill
a fly on the wall". Perhaps some simpler (single) imputation methods would
still be viable, having in mind that outgoing ties of not more than 7%
actors are missing?

Kind regards,
Marko Luci?

P.S. Not entirely related to the problem above, I saw that Koskinen, Robins
and Pattison (2013) mention some "freely available software" to illustrate
their Bayesian approach to data augmentation. I wasn't able to find this
software on the web, so can any of you please provide me with a link if it
is available?

> Your suggestion is in line with the work by Wang et al 2016 (attached). It

> all imputed data sets are imputed with the same parameters. For proper
> imputation you need to draw the parameters from an estimated posterior (in
> non network settings you could also do bootstrapping). Otherwise you will
> underestimate the between imputation variance (obtaining the proper
> standard errors for the effects after multiple imputation is a bit more
> complicated than taking the mean of the estimated models - see the attached
> paper by Schafer and Graham, 2002, page 19/20).
> You can solve this problem by utilizing the method by Koskinen et al.
> (2013) that you mentioned.
> It is available in the PNet software. I attached an adaptation of it for
> R. It requires the packages Bergm and igraph. (Please note that this is NOT
> Johan Koskinen's R script but an adaptation of his R-script, in which I
> implemented the missing data treatment within the normal Bergm estimation.
> I do not know where, you can find his script on the web, but you can get it
> from him via email.)
>
> However, you are absolutely right, that you still have the problem that
> your actual model would not be the imputation model and that the
> imputations might not preserve the relationships between the networks
> properly.
> I have never run a multiplex ERGM. If you can run a multiplex ERGM with
> the ergm package in R, then it should be straight forward to adapt the
> Bergm code to impute all of the networks properly.
> If you do this and your interest is in the model parameters, you will not
> need multiple imputation. The estimated posteriors that you will get from
> the Bergm estimation should be (asymptotically) identical to multiple
> imputation. The procedure imputes the missing data at every iteration and
> uses the new imputed network for the next parameter estimation. Running 50
> or so additional ERGMs or BERGMs will not provide you with better parameter
> or standard error estimates. If you cannot run a multiplex ERGM but you are
> "just" using the other networks as covariates, it is possible to write your

> change. This is also in line with the results from Huisman & Steglich 2008
> on SAOMs, you can see there that with 20% missing data, the bias in
> parameter estimation is quite low. Of course SAOMs and ERGMs are a
> different model family, but they are both network models...
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marko,

Good to hear that it works.

To your question: If you want to impute the data in your focal network, but
you also have missing data in the covariates, the missing in the covariates
must also be imputed. These imputations should always maintain the
relationships between all of your networks. One way to do it is as the MICE
package does it (multiple imputation by chained equation). Now, MICE does
not handle networks, but the algorithm could look like this: Assuming we
have 4 networks: The idea is to first impute the missing values in all
networks (or all but 1) with an initial guess (e.g. overall density), then
we impute the first network once, taking all the other networks as
covariates. Then we impute network number 2, taking the other networks (3 &
4) as covariate and also taking the *imputed *network 1 as covariate. We
continue this procedure, next imputing network 3 with network 4 and the
imputed networks 1 & 2 as covariate. Once all networks are imputed we just
start again, this time taking the imputed networks as covariate... Of
course you could also have non-network covariates, you can impute those
with (logistic) regression at any point in this procedure.
This of course needs to run very long (and I would not be surprised if this
means a day or two) until it is converged. You can then either sample
networks from the converged chain to get your imputations, or, if you saved
the parameters during this process, you actually have a multiplex model and
you can just interpret these posteriors.
That is what I meant with: * write your own multiplex analyses for Bergms.*
I have never tried this, but theoretically, it should work (if not, I hope
that someone on this list will point out the falut in my idea).

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Using GPU processing for ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Juan,

I am aware of some work trying to parallelise various aspects of ERGM MCMC sampling (beyond the trivial one of running multiple independent chains in parallel), but I am not aware of any resounding successes thus far, and none with GPUs. Part of the problem is that while it's often possible to split up the space of possible Metropolis-Hastings proposals in such a way that their acceptances and rejections are mutually independent,

  *   this is only possible to do efficiently if there is a Markov conditional dependence structure (which often leads to bad models);
  *   for less restrictive structures, there would be significant overhead in calculating what is independent of what; and
  *   after every acceptance or rejection, all the results would need to be collated, so the pipeline for each GPU would be very short.

Best,
Pavel
